rationale: We own three shares, bought two days ago at $251.85, and the stock is down about 7.4% since. A two-day price move tells me nothing about the business, and I don't sell a good business because Mr. Market is in a mood. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of about 26.9%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and owner earnings of roughly $9.26 billion against a $140 billion market cap. Its DCF says $437.57 a share against a price of $233.26, but that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat the margin of safety as generous rather than gospel. What keeps me from adding with conviction is that the snapshot has no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure and no moat metrics, and the durability of a switching-cost moat in a fast-changing field is the question I must keep asking. I keep the position, size it modestly, and let the facts come in.

rationale: I can explain how Best Buy makes money: it buys consumer electronics and appliances from a few big suppliers and resells them at thin margins. But I cannot find a moat I would bet ten years on. The same products can be bought online from rivals, and the suppliers can sell direct. The numbers in front of me look decent, with a 5-year average ROE of 48.4% and debt-to-equity of 0.37. But a ROE that high on a retailer may reflect a shrunken equity base as much as franchise strength, and the snapshot gives me nothing to check that. The 15.6% margin of safety only just clears my bar, and it rests on zero growth and a 5% discount rate, so a slight change in assumptions erases it. I would rather wait for a business with pricing power than pay a fair price for a hard-fought retail margin, so I pass.

exit_trigger: Not applicable; no position is taken; Would revisit only if a full business description, a 10-year earnings record and management history showed a durable moat inside my circle
rationale: I don't own this one, and I'm going to pass. The numbers on the page are attractive: a 5-year average ROE of 22.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.43, and a price of $42.40 against a computed value of $75.94. But the snapshot gives me no description of the business, no earnings history, and no management record. Without those I can't say with confidence how it makes money or whether its moat will last ten years. A stock that looks cheap on a spreadsheet, in a field where the competitive ground may be shifting under it, is how I've lost money before. A 44% discount is no comfort if I can't tell whether the earnings power will be there in 2036. I'd rather miss this pitch than swing at one I can't see clearly. Invert: what could go wrong? Technology could erode the franchise, and I can't rule that out from here.

rationale: I own this one, so the question is whether the reason I bought it is still intact, not whether to open a position. The shares are down 16.04% from my entry at 128.38, but price decline alone is never a reason to sell. The record in front of me is a 5-year average ROE of 34.6% with debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, which is what a franchise with pricing power looks like. The model's intrinsic value of about $363 per share rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on it. Even a much more conservative number leaves room, so I keep what I own. My real worry is whether an apparel brand is a durable moat or a fashion cycle, and nothing in this snapshot settles that. I will not add until I can verify the earnings history and the brand's pricing power.

exit_trigger: Return on equity falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years, signalling moat erosion; Negative annual operating cash flow, a sign of management or business failure; Price above 1.5x owner-earnings intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Evidence that AI-driven competitors are forcing price cuts or subscriber losses
rationale: I don't own Adobe, and this is a buy-or-wait question. I understand the business: creative and document software that people pay for by subscription, and that professionals have built their workflows around. On the snapshot, the numbers are attractive. The market cap is about $90.0 billion, five-year average ROE is 40.0%, debt-to-equity is 0.41, and the model's intrinsic value of $467.50 sits well above the $231.22 price. But a 5% discount rate and 8% growth produce a flattering number, and the snapshot doesn't let me test the thing that matters most, which is whether this moat survives a decade of rapid change in AI-generated content. It also doesn't show ten years of earnings, CEO tenure, or customer retention. Add a book that already holds ten names, and I'd rather wait than buy a cheap-looking price on faith. If the missing evidence confirms pricing power and retention, I'd want to own this.

exit_trigger: Moat erosion: five-year ROE falls clearly below 15%, or the franchise test fails in a majority of recent years; Management failure: negative annual operating cash flow, restatement, or value-destroying acquisitions; Franchise-law reform or manufacturer direct sales that structurally strip dealers of service and parts economics; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value and staying there
rationale: I own this one, six shares at $216.765 bought in August, and I'm down about 2% after 103 days, which tells me nothing. A car dealer is a business I understand: it sells cars, services them, finances them, and earns its keep on parts and service. The numbers I can see are good: a five-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.40, a $13.9 billion market cap, and a price about 18% below the owner-earnings value of $260 a share. That cushion clears my 15% bar, but not by a wide margin, and the valuation assumes zero growth. The moat is the part I hold loosely, since it rests mostly on state franchise laws and the scale of the operation, not on a brand that makes customers pay more. I'll keep what I own, not add until I can verify the ten-year earnings record and management's record, and I'll sell only if the franchise economics erode, never because the quote wobbles.

exit_trigger: 5-year ROE falls below 15% in a sustained way (moat erosion); Negative annual operating cash flow or evidence of management dishonesty; Price exceeds 1.5x intrinsic value (about $626/share) persistently; Loss of a major franchise program or a shift in government procurement that weakens the competitive position
rationale: I own General Dynamics, and the question is whether to keep it. The snapshot gives a 5-year average ROE of 17.2% and a debt-to-equity of 0.32, both inside my thresholds, and a margin of safety of 16.4%, just over my 15% bar, on an owner-earnings DCF with growth capped at 8% and a 5% discount rate. The moat is regulatory and intangible: submarines and other defense platforms where the government has few alternative suppliers and qualification barriers are high. It is not a Coca-Cola, and I cannot see in this snapshot the margin or backlog detail that would tell me how much pricing power exists. I paid $353.20 and the shares are down 1.2% after 21 days, which is noise to me, so I keep the position. I would not add aggressively on this evidence alone, because the margin of safety is thin and several of my checks could not be performed from these data.

exit_trigger: Moat erosion: ROE falls persistently below 15%, showing the franchise no longer earns above-average returns; Management failure: negative operating cash flow, restatements, or value-destroying acquisitions; Price persistently above 1.5 times intrinsic value; A durable technology or channel shift that undermines the brand's pricing power
rationale: I own this one, and nothing in front of me gives me a reason to change that. A water heater is a distress purchase. The homeowner wants the plumber to install something that works and will not come back, and a trusted brand sold through the trade channel is a modest but real moat. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.7% with debt-to-equity of 0.37, and an owner-earnings DCF value of $98.59 against a $63.61 price, a 36.2% margin of safety. I would add that the DCF uses a 5% discount rate, which flatters the answer, so I will not lean on the precise number. We are only 26 days in, up 3.42%, and my favorite holding period is forever, so I keep the shares and let the business do the work. I cannot check the ten-year earnings record, CEO tenure or insider activity from this snapshot, so I will not add until I can.
